utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Can we have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to apologise for this delay. The day has been extremely busy. We are going to resume with the new witness. Will it be Mr. Hayman? Let us have the witness brought in, please. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you please give us your name, your first name, your current status, your professional status, your domicile, and after that we will ask you to remain standing for a few moments in order to take the solemn declaration. First of all, your name and your first name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Matthew Dundas-Whatley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Dundas-Whatley; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is your profession and current residence, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm currently in business in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. The usher is going to give you the solemn declaration, that is your oath. Please read it while you are still standing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much, Mr. Whatley, please be seated. You have been called to appear, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, by the Defence for General Blaskic in the trial which is being conducted by the Prosecution. You are at the International Criminal Tribunal. Please speak freely, you are under oath. First you will answer the questions that the party which has called you in will ask you, that is the Defence, and then you will be asked questions by the Office of the Prosecutor, and finally the Judges will have questions to ask you. Mr. Dundas-Whatley, Mr. Hayman, we didn't get the summary, but we will do it for the next witness; but since we used a lot of time up we will dispense with that and ask you to begin. I have the summary here. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Hayman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Whatley, you are a former officer of the British army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe your military career of service to the Court?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: I did approximately eight years with the British army, and this started in 1985 where I attended a three-day officer selection course. And when I passed that, I then went to the Royal Military Academy at Sandhurst where I trained for nearly a year to become a British army officer. At the completion of that course I joined my regiment, and then for the next six years or so I was posted in various countries in the world. I rose to the rank of captain, and my final job in the army was in Bosnia. During my nearly eight years in the army I attended many training courses in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to your regiment, are you referring to the Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your position in the regiment at the time the regiment was ordered to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: I was selected by my commanding officer, Bob Stewart, to be a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will pause slightly after your answers, and if you could do the same so the translators can complete their work. Before you were selected by Colonel Stewart to be a liaison officer during the regiment's tour of service in Bosnia, what had your position been in the regiment?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: In the two years leading up to deployment to Bosnia I had been the training officer, the operations officer, and the second in command of a company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your tour of service in Bosnia, did you leave the British army?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And under what circumstances did you leave the army?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: The army underwent a large scale reduction in force, and that's when I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any medals or other recognition for your service in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I got the United Nations Bosnia Medal, and I was mentioned in dispatches by the British government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you received any prior medals for your service with the British army?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I got the British Northern Ireland Medal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left the British army in roughly 1993, what was your employment?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: I went back to the former Yugoslavia as a humanitarian aid worker, firstly with a British NGO in Belgrade, an organisation called OXFAM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say NGO, can you tell the Court what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: NGO means non-governmental organisation, charity. I worked in Belgrade about seven months. I then went back to Bosnia and worked in another British NGO called "Feed the Children" for about ten months, and then I did some consulting work with another British NGO helping old people in Mostar. After that, towards the middle of 1995, I then went into business and self-employment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left "Feed the Children" what was your position with that relief organisation?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Within two weeks of arriving with "Feed the Children" I was promoted to be what was called the Bosnia coordinator, which meant I was the director for all their operations in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us turn to your tour, or service, of duty in Bosnia-Herzegovina with the Cheshire Regiment. Did the regiment receive any special training prior to its deployment to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, we did. The training for most of the regiment I think lasted for about two months and took place in Germany, because that is where it was based at the time; but for me, I only had about two weeks training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Because I was part of the advance party. In fact, I was part of what we call the pre-advance party into Bosnia on October the 16th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a large map to your right on the easel, it is Exhibit -- strike that. Let's use that map, Exhibit 29, if you would, there should also be a pointer in front of you, and my question for you is how the liaison officers for the Cheshire Regiment, which as we know in this Court was principally based in Vitez, but also with detachments in Tuzla and Gornji Vakuf; could you first tell us, and if it is helpful, show the Court on the map how the Cheshire Regiment divided the responsibilities of the various liaison officers for the regiment?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to work out how best to do this with the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a microphone that can be moved and made more convenient, and you may well need to stand in order to point to the map. First, perhaps you could tell the Court, and if it is helpful, point out the locations involved.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I point to the map probably the best thing to do, to start with, is explain the concept by which the liaison officers were created and for what purpose. Colonel Bob Stewart decided it was very important, for him to be successful as the commander of the British forces in Bosnia, that he had to have a very good understanding and a very good liaison with the military commanders fighting the war. Because our main mission, as given to us by the United Nations, was primarily to be concerned with transporting of food and escorting convoys into Bosnia. And so, he dedicated five captains, including myself, with the task of keeping a constant liaison with those people, the local commanders, and at the same time, of course, he had to deploy the battalion around Bosnia. The way he did that was by putting a company down in Gornji Vakuf, a company in Vitez, and a company in Tuzla, and put with each of those some one or two liaison officers. Two of us liaison officers were based in Vitez, I was one of them. So, if I could now just go to the map. This is the town of Gornji Vakuf, down here, where we stationed one liaison officer. This is the town of Vitez, where I was stationed, and one other captain. And the Tuzla is off the map, up here, where two more captains were stationed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if Exhibit 183/1 could be placed on the ELMO, please. I think you may be seated. If we could zoom in a little more on the map. Thank you very much to the technical staff. Using this map, if it's helpful, and you may point on the ELMO, and then your indications will be indicated on the video monitors throughout the courtroom, what your initial area of responsibility was as a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: The two liaison officers based here in Vitez, myself and one other, our area of responsibility did not extend into the purple, but limited to the green and yellow. Of course, my first, my initial area of responsibility was what we call the Maglaj finger, because there is the town of Maglaj, right down -- sorry, I moved it -- right down to a sort of shape like this. The southernmost city was there in my initial area, which was the city of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, roughly it included the area stretching from Maglaj to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: I can list the towns, if you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: The towns in my initial area of responsibility were Maglaj, Zepce, Zavidovici, Tesanj and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tour of duty, first, did you have occasion to cover other areas due to the absence from the theatre of the other liaison officer based in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, the arrangement made from the beginning is the other captain and I would shadow each other's responsibilities. If he needed support for something I would come in and cover him, and vice versa, and when he went on leave I would cover his area. And so, from the very beginning I developed a very good understanding of his area, and he of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he take any leaves or other absences during the tour of duty that required you to cover his area of responsibility on a more full-time basis?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, he was away for two weeks in December, '92, so I covered him during that period; and then he went back to the United Kingdom in the first week of March, '93, and so I then moved down permanently and covered his area from then until May the 16th when I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what area was it that you took over in early March, 1993 from this other liaison officer who departed?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: I will point it out on the map for you. It was the towns of Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, and I also retained responsibility for Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You touched on this briefly, but could you tell the Court anything more concerning the principal duty or duties of the liaison officers for the Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: The primary responsibility of the liaison officers, as defined by Colonel Bob Stewart, was that we should maintain a constant link with the military commanders, that we should be the passage, or we should be the route through which information would flow to UNPROFOR from the local factions, and to the warring factions from UNPROFOR, that we had to develop a very close relationship with the commanders, and indeed, on occasions with the civilian leaders, develop a very close relationship with them. And in our case it was mainly the Bosnian army and the HVO, but on occasions with the Serbs. We also had additional duties, but I must stress that was our overriding duty. Additional duties were in the information collection areas, where we were expected to gather a substantial amount of information about the activities and structures of the local warring factions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have mentioned several different tasks; were any of those multiple tasks in conflict?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: It wasn't a conflict that was difficult to handle, but it is important to point out, I think, that maintaining the trust and maintaining the integrity of ourselves when dealing with the local commanders, required, quite logically, that we were not seen as spies. And so, any information that we were given, which was on occasions quite substantial, by one side, we did not pass to the other, but we kept it within the United Nations information chain. And so, there was a certain conflict there that we didn't want to be seen to be spies, and so we didn't ask hundreds and hundreds of questions about the details of their military command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How frequent was your contact with commanders in the warring parties, the Bosnian army and the HVO, during your work?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: From the day I arrived until the day I left that was my only task, and I was out at least six days a week, and quite often for 12, 15 hours, dealing only with local military commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the liaison officers for the regiment have more contact with the commanders of the warring parties than others in the regiment?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, by far. The liaison officers and the commanding officer were probably the only people that had any detailed meetings with any of the local military commanders. It was our full-time job. Colonel Bob Stewart also took part in very important meetings with very senior commanders. But that was, we were out there the whole time and very few members of the regiment had the contact that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the commanding officer of the regiment, and perhaps other senior officers, obtain information from the liaison officers about the warring parties? And if so, how?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: The way it worked was that we would leave in the morning on our duties and come back at the end of the day. If during that time, or in fact at any time, we discovered information that was considered vital, that would probably be radioed through straight away; but more routinely at the end of the day we returned to our base in Vitez, and if I had information that was very important but sensitive, I would go to Colonel Stewart's office and brief him personally. Or alternatively, and this happened routinely, every day, I would be debriefed by the military information office. In addition, at five o'clock every evening we had a conference where I was expected to speak about my activities that day for the general audience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the audience at that 5.00 p.m. daily briefing?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: The senior officers of the regiment and the heads of department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the MILINFOSUM; what product did they produce, and to whom was it sent?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Every evening the military information office produced a MILINFOSUM, which is a military information summary, this was produced every day in the evening by the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to whom was it sent?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: The MILINFOSUM was transmitted firstly to Kiseljak, which was the headquarters of UNPROFOR in Bosnia. In addition it was sent to Split, which was the headquarters of the British forces in the former Yugoslavia. And I believe it was also sent directly to Britain, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the meetings and contacts you had with commanders of the warring factions, did you also have contact with lower level soldiers in the BH army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: On a lower level my contact with the local warring factions was checkpoints just like every other member of the battalion who was travelling around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you travel a lot?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I travelled a lot around Bosnia, and I travelled through a lot of checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you were travelling on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: All the time, every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to answer the following question without divulging any information that might be considered sensitive or confidential. Did the British Battalion have an intelligence apparatus in Bosnia-Herzegovina of the type it would have were it to be at war with an enemy?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: The British army trains for war, and I spent many years training for war, and when the British army goes to war, like I believe all NATO armies, it takes with it a large intelligence gathering network. To give you some idea how this would work, in the British situation it would normally be run by the intelligence corps, which is a department in the army, and it would have an enormous array of assets for the purpose of gathering information about the enemy; such things as satellites, spy planes, equipment for listening to the enemy's radio networks and decoding them. We would conduct reconnaissance into enemy territory, and we would conduct research into the background of the personalities commanding the enemy. We would use radar for spotting artillery and mortars, and the information from that would all form part of the intelligence collection which is vital in the commander's plan for future operations. In the case of Bosnia, we didn't have anything like that. In the case of Bosnia we were not at war. We had a military information office which I believe had two members of staff, or possibly three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result, was there a difference between the amount of information the British battalion received about the BH army and the HVO from what it would have received had it been at war with either one of those parties?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think the quantity of the information is at issue here, it's the type -- it's the information -- it's the type of information that we were looking for and that we needed to conduct our business. So you cannot really compare what we were doing in Bosnia with what we would do in war, if we went to war against the HVO or the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me to ask you to think back to your first arrival in Bosnia in October 1992, and ask you whether you, to your knowledge, your colleagues in the British battalion, did you have any preconceptions about the war and the parties to the conflict when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: We were the first regiment in from the British army, and so consequently there was no -- there was not a great deal of information available to us before we went in, and we relied almost entirely upon newspaper and television articles. So we built up an impression in our minds, I think, which became our established feelings prior to our arrival in Bosnia. And the feeling we had then, back in October '92, was that Bosnia-Herzegovina had a government in Sarajevo, and this government, with its own assets, was at war against a very large Serb army which had rebelled against the authority of that government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in country, did you find that there was also a conflict between the BH army and the HVO in progress?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, there was. We were not aware of this before we arrived, and it was on October 18th, two days after I arrived in Split, on October 18th, after I travelled for the first time into middle Bosnia, and if I can refer to the map I can explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, you're referring to Exhibit 29. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: The route we travelled up to get into middle Bosnia, this was in a Land Rover convoy of about, I think, seven or eight Land Rovers, took us over the mountains along roads which in the main were not made up, were not covered with tarmac. We went past the lake here Ramsko Lake, through the town of Prozor here which was very tense, up over the mountain and down the hill into Gorini Vakuf here, which was nice and peaceful and quiet. We then went up north here, up a valley road, a very badly made road. And when we got into this high area here. This is when we began to realise that the problems in Bosnia were extended beyond just a Serb problem. We went from checkpoint to checkpoint to checkpoint. Prior to arriving in Prozor, I think we had been through one or two checkpoints over the first hundred miles of the journey. Here the checkpoints were every mile or every two miles. Some of the badges had "TO" on them, and some of the soldiers had no badges and there were the occasional HVO badges. It was rather difficult to tell from the way they were dressed exactly what was going on, but we had an interpreter. At all these checkpoints we discussed what was going on, and if I could very quickly explain what was happening. Most of this area at the time, most of this area was in the control of the TO, the Territorial Defence, but some of the villages were Croat villages, and they didn't consider themselves to be under the control of the Territorial Defence, but under their own control, the Croat control. When we got further north to Novi Travnik, we left this village problem behind and things changed again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you and your colleagues arrived in country, what then was your initial impression of the HVO's relationship to this problem as you defined it, that being a central government and a Serb rebellion. How did the HVO fit into the initial thinking, at least on your part, and perhaps if you can tell us, your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Certainly in those first few days, first two days probably, we felt that the HVO was a rebel organisation, that it was fighting against the established government in Sarajevo, and it was a traitor, it was a rebel organisation. That's how we felt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of your contacts with the BH army and the HVO, after a period of weeks or months did you come to have a different understanding of the problem?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes. After a few months in the country and spending all my time talking to military commanders and civil leaders, we began to see the situation rather differently. We began to see Bosnia being made up of three separate people with three separate armies, three separate military structures and civilian structures, and all three of them were united in their own national connection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned these checkpoints on the road between Gornji Vakuf and Novi Travnik. Was there a pattern to the checkpoints, or was there a purpose that you could discern to the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: That was our first encounter with checkpoints. The situation there was not unique at all. The situation there had arisen as a result of enormous mistrust between the Muslim villages and the Croat villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your initial tour of duty did you keep a diary?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you the following question, and if you need to refer to your diary, with the Court's permission you may, whether in the latter part of October did you make a determination under whose control the road south from Novi Travnik towards Gornji Vakuf was, that is who controlled that road?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I've just described to you the situation as we found it on the 18th of October. If I could now refer to my diary of Saturday the 24th of October.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: 1992. And if I could read it to you. "My vehicle, followed by as Ander's Toyota, then Olie Halstead's, very few roadblocks compared with last time," I'm referring to the days before, “The Novi Travnik road is indisputably in TO hands."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on your almost daily contacts with HVO commanders and HVO commands during late 1992 and in early 1993, can you tell the Court what type of army was the HVO as you saw it, and understood it and came to understand it?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: The HVO and the Bosnian army, in my opinion, were both peasant armies. They were made up of villagers, most of whom had probably had experience in the Yugoslav army as conscripts, but they were ill-disciplined, they were drinking on the streets. And they were organised on a territorial village-by-village basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the court what the consequences of that were, being organised on a territorial basis as you put it, village-by-village basis?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: The result of being organised in that way was the loyalties of the soldiers were to the village, to the local leaders and the local politicians, that the -- that they were primarily concerned with the defence of the village. And dealing with small units of this nature whose raison d’être was defence of the village, it was almost impossible and very difficult at least to organise them into what we would call a military command structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why would the presence of these predominantly local loyalties, as you put it, undermine the creation of a military chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: There was a conflict of interests between defending the village you're living in and operating in a greater or a grander military scheme, which may require you to have to leave your village under the command of somebody you've never met and go and fight somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You've mentioned the chain of command, and I'd like to take a short detour from the events of your tour of duty, and I would ask for assistance in placing an exhibit on the ELMO and distributing it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D414.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have before you on the ELMO Exhibit D414, and my question for you is: You've mentioned chain of command. Can you tell us, in the British army system, what is the chain of command from the level of brigade commander down?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: When we talk about the chain of command in the British army, we're talking about from one headquarters to a subordinate one. In the case of this chart here, we have a brigade headquarters here commanded by a Brigadier. Under need him we have four or five battalions, each of which will be commanded, in the British system, by a Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the technical booth zoom in on the picture slightly, please? Thank you. Please continue?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: And under each one of those battalions, under each one you could expect another four or five companies, each commanded by a Major. So the chain of command would go from the Brigadier, to the Lieutenant-Colonel to the Major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within that structure, who are the commanders? Who would be known as a commander?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Commanders are the -- at the brigade level with the Brigadier. In American it would be known as a one-star General. At the battalion level it is the Lieutenant-Colonel and at the company level it is the Major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this chart -- by the way, did you design this chart?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I thought it might help explain the confusion here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a box to the right of the brigade labelled "Brigade Staff Officers". Who are, and are Brigade Staff Officers commanders?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Brigade Staff Officers are not commanders. The Brigade Staff Officers work for the Brigadier. They are obviously junior to him in rank, Colonels, Majors, Captains, and they are his specialists in various fields and they advise him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What types of duties or areas would a Brigade Staff Officer have responsibility over?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Generally -- of course, every brigade is different with different purposes, but generally there will be a chief of staff who at brigade level in the British system would probably be a Major. And then there will be probably maybe another Major dealing with the administration side of life or re-supply. There will be a Captain -- or probably a Captain dealing with intelligence and another Captain dealing with the operations. There will probably be, depending on the side of the brigade and its purpose, you'll have communications officers and transport officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to return to your tour of duty and your observations of the HVO. Could you tell the court how the HVO differed from the British army?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: It's very difficult to compare the HVO with the British army. The British army has a highly organised structure developed over many years, and within that structure the commanders and the units have a well-defined relationship based on training and respect, and it's well understood throughout the whole system. In the case of the HVO, that isn't exist. The HVO was formed during the war, out of chaos, and the structures were developed from the village upwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other differences that you noted as a result of your observations?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Another probably important factor is to compare the command structure and the rank structure of the British army with the HVO. In the British army, officers and soldiers, senior NCOs, belong to a meritocracy where they are promoted as a result of being good at their job, getting good reports. In the case of the HVO, people were given appointments overnight, and people, who before the war had almost no responsibility at all, found themselves as brigade commanders. A very good example of this would be commander Mario Cerkez, who commanded the Vitez Brigade in the time I was there, in the HVO. Before the war, I believe he had been a security guard in the local ammunition factory and here he was, with very little military experience and very little education, commanding the Vitez Brigade of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the exhibit which I think is still on the ELMO, D414, we see a Brigadier who would command a brigade in the British army. What type of experience, or training or selection process would entitle someone in the British army system to command a brigade?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: A British brigade commander would typically have about 25 years of professional, full-time military training with many, many courses probably in that time, with three or four years spent away on courses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said 25 years of training. Did you mean 25 years of experience with the training courses you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other differences you noted between the British army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I think we should look -- it's important to look at the equipment which the HVO had. When the British army trains and when the British army goes to war, it is equipped with all the military equipment required to fight that war. Communications equipment, logistical equipment, re-supply equipment, military hardware, artillery regiments, tank regiments, aeroplanes, helicopters and this type of thing, radar systems. The HVO had none of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the HVO properly equipped to fight a modern war or fight war in the modern style?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: In middle Bosnia where I dealt with the HVO, and I can only speak for middle Bosnia, there were very few tanks, very little artillery in the HVO. It was fighting a war in the late 20th Century in the style which we were fighting a hundred years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it you would say something similar with respect to the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It was exactly the same with the Bosnian army as well. There is one other area where I think I could -- I think it makes it so difficult to compare the HVO with the Bosnian army, and I've alluded to it already, but I think I should go into a little bit more detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said HVO and Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, HVO and the British army. And this was in the area of how people were selected and trained for their positions. I've already mentioned one example, but across the board, in the British army, soldiers are selected, trained and promoted over a period of time within a structure for the purposes of conducting -- of carrying out a job, and over the period of their careers, whether they're in the army for three years or 30 years, that is an ongoing process. In the case of the HVO, the men were mobilised from the villages, from the streets, given a rifle and told to get on with it. For those reasons, I don't think you can really compare the HVO or the Bosnian army with the British army or any other NATO army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the role of training in building a professional army. Did you, during your six-month or so tour of duty, did you ever see HVO troops engaged in training?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On any occasions?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: No, I didn't. And in the time I was in -- in the time that I was in Bosnia, I never heard anyone else talk about the training of either the HVO or the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the HVO a disciplined, organised military force or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: No, it was not a -- in my experience in middle Bosnia, the HVO and the Bosnian army were not disciplined and well-organised military forces. This information was -- came to us as a result of their own commanders telling us of the problems that they had controlling the rogue gangs that they had as soldiers and units underneath them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO have a large headquarters well equipped with staff? And I'm referring to the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: We did not know -- or I did not know how many trained staff officers they had in their headquarters. In order to evaluate the ability of their headquarters, we would need to -- we would need to know that, but I've already given you some idea of how many trained staff officers we would have in a British brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would a British brigade headquarters have any type of communications unit?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Depending on its role, but it could expect to have probably a signals squadron working within the brigade. And it should be stressed also that I've been talking about a brigade headquarters. In the case of Hotel Vitez, there were many brigades under the command of that headquarters. It was more of -- by the British standard you could say a divisional command or even higher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it your testimony is you're not able to answer the question whether the HVO headquarters in Central Bosnia was -- functioned well or functioned professionally because you do not know how many professionally trained officers they had in their headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO headquarters in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone have access to secure fax or other secure communications?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, and our dealings with them were over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it dangerous to use unsecured communications in a military headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it would be very dangerous to try to prosecute a war at that level without access and without the use of secure communications. And the reasons for this are that any radio transmissions or telephone transmissions which are not coded can, of course, be -- would probably be picked up by the enemy, your enemy. In that situation, if you are giving instructions to your subordinate units, your subordinate brigades, orders of what they are required to do, if the enemy heard those orders, the enemy would have a very good understanding of your intentions. And in the same way, if the subordinate units were then reporting to you and telling them how they're getting on, have they taken any land, have they taken any casualties, have they lost any land, that information, if that information went into enemy hands they would have a very good understanding of where your strengths and weaknesses were. So to operate without secure communications, on that level, is very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR use any secure communications?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: I don't believe we did, but we were not -- certainly at the level I operated no, we did not, and, in fact, we made no secret of our radio frequencies, but we were not fighting a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it it was by design that UNPROFOR did not attempt to shield their communications?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: I don't know the reasons why we weren't given secure communications, but it was not important for what we were doing, because we were not fighting a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention forward in time to April or perhaps March of 1993. At this time, I take it, you were the sole liaison officer responsible for the areas of Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca and Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes. In March and up to about the middle of April I was the sole liaison officer for that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to April of 1993, did an entity known as the 7th Muslim Brigade come to your attention, and if so, in what regard?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: The organisation which became known as the 7th Muslim Brigade came to our attention -- came to my attention in about January 1993. It had rather a destabilising effect from the moment we were aware of it, and it is because of how destabilising it was that it was brought to our attention that it existed. The 7th Muslim Brigade was formed, I believe, and it was what I believed at the time and I have no reason not to believe it now, in a village called Nemila, which I shall point out on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're pointing above the map Exhibit 29; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, your map is not big enough for the purpose of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it some place north of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I believe about 15 kilometres north, and it was known to us as the Nemila Brigade originally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the characteristics that were reported to the British battalion concerning this brigade?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: The 7th Muslim Brigade represented a new dimension in the way the war -- the military situation was going in middle Bosnia. They were paid as soldiers and they were paid quite well. This was unusual, because most of the normal Bosnian army, which attracted most of the Muslims, were not paid or were paid an absolute pittance. In addition to being well paid, they were well equipped. Instead of having to share rifles they had one each, and they were given proper uniforms. In addition to all this, they were also expected to stop drinking and to attend the mosque, and most Bosnian Muslims do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they were paid more, that is the members of the 7th Muslim Brigade received higher pay or salary than other BH army officers. Was it known where these funds were coming from to pay members of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Of course, we never knew anything about them for definite, but what we did -- what we were told is that the money came from the Middle East, and the effect of paying these soldiers was that it attracted soldiers away from the normal Bosnian army units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that soldiers actually left the existing BH army units and joined 7th Muslim Brigade as sort of as a competitor of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: That's what we believed at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the 7th Muslim Brigade had a destabilising effect on the military situation in Central Bosnia. Why and how did it have a destabilising effect?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: To answer that question I'd like to use Travnik as an example. I'll just point it out. Prior to the war, Travnik -- the populations of Muslims and Croats in the town of Travnik were roughly equal, and the relationship in the town was very good. And then as a result of the war there was a huge influx of Muslim refugees from Serb territory. This upset the balance of population in the town enormously, and at the time we believed that the Croats were probably out numbered by between three to one and six to one in the town. But the commanders of the Bosnian army in the town, and the HVO in the town, maintained the alliance, Colonel Alagic and Colonel Filipovic; Alagic from the Bosnian army, and Filipovic from the HVO. And they did everything they could to maintain the alliance and not let the destabilising effects of a huge influx of refugees detract from their ability to prosecute the war against the Serbs. But then, probably in about March 1993, and I don't remember the date, the 7th Muslim Brigade opened an office in the town and started attracting soldiers to join them, you could hear, you could see them in their slightly different uniforms. This introduced a different type of nationalism and different type of religious fundamentalism which had not existed in Travnik in the thousand year history of the town. The Croats in the town were very frightened, as were the normal moderate Muslims. This is not what they expected. But when I questioned the Bosnian army commanders about this, they told me the 7th Muslim Brigade was not under their control. Its very presence had a worrying effect on the Bosnian army commanders, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the presence of the 7th Muslim Brigade, for example, in Travnik, did it become an issue among politicians in the town?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: In the sense that -- yes, it did, in the sense that the Croat politicians used the presence of these extreme Muslims, dressing slightly differently, to raise the, to raise the nationalist feelings of the Croats in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that, are you thinking of a particular politician in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: During -- yes, there is a very good example, the details of which I do not remember properly, but I do remember a visit to the town by Mate Boban, who was the president of, I believe the president of Herceg-Bosna at the time. As a result of his visit the tension between the -- or shall I say not necessarily as a result of his visit, but after his visit, the tension in the town and the relationship between the Muslims and the Croats in the town deteriorated rapidly; and there were incidents of flag burning in the town, burning of Croat flags and of Bosnian flags.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the 7th Muslim Brigade present in any other locations in Central Bosnia other than Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, before they moved to Travnik, I have already pointed out the village of Nemila, where we believe they started; but they were in other towns, as well. And if you like I can point them out on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can tell us or point out on the map where else they established units.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Further north, this is the city of Zenica here, further north I've already pointed out the, approximately here, the village of Nemila, where we first heard of this brigade. Further north to that, there were the towns of Zepce and Zavidovici, which unfortunately, again, are not on this map. It was in Zepce that I first became aware of the 7th Muslim Brigade. So, we had Nemila, Zepce, Zavidovici, and later on we had Travnik, Novi Travnik, down here approximately here, there is a place called Ravno Rostovo, which is not even a village, it's a collection of houses on this mountain here. And over here the town of Kakanj. Those were the locations that I was aware that the 7th Muslim Brigade had offices and units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this in the first three or four months of 1993 that this unit or these units seemed to be springing up in the region?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think it probably all started at about Christmas time, and by the end of March, the situation was as I described just then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any more specific information concerning the presence of the 7th Muslim Brigade in the town of Zepce?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Zepce was the town much further north on the map, which in January 1993 that I first came face-to-face with the 7th Muslim Brigade. As a liaison officer for the town I always visited both the Bosnian headquarters and the headquarters of the HVO in the town. And on one occasion, and I do not remember the date, both commanders told me exactly the same thing; and they told me that we are very worried, there is a new unit in this town. Now, I should point out that the commander of the Bosnian army was a Muslim and a commander of the HVO was a Croat, but they were both very concerned about this new unit. And I went to have a look, and the 7th Muslim Brigade had taken over a building opposite the command headquarters of the HVO, and they had erected a flagpole, and on the top of the flagpole was a green flag with the crescent moon and the star, which is associated with Islam. The Croats, the HVO considered this to be very antagonistic in the middle of the town, in a town which boasted of having a mosque, a Catholic church and an Orthodox church all together in a straight line. And they considered this to be antagonistic. But also, the Bosnian army commander told me it was antagonistic. He also told me he could not command them, they were not under his command, and he also told me he was losing some of his soldiers who were going to join them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there later fighting in Zepce?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, after, I think in about May there was very bad fighting in the town of Zepce, and the result was it became a Croat enclave and all the Muslims were kicked out of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the fighting in Central Bosnia in the January 1993 time period, and perhaps it was early February, was there a cease-fire of some sort ordered?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think, yes, there was, I know what you're referring to, there was a cease-fire, I think at the end of January. I can't remember, it may have been in the 3rd or 4th week of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher in distributing a document, Mr. President. There is an original and BCS and a hand-written English translation. We have no French translation at this time, Mr. President, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D415, 415A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you could examine that document, and while we're doing that I would ask that a map be marked and placed on the ELMO. It's a standard Zenica 4 JNA map, and there are certain portions highlighted which I think will fit on the ELMO so they can be visibly seen. But first it needs to be marked as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to Exhibit D415A, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately when did you first see it?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Probably on the day it was written, certainly it would either have been that day or the day after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive both D415 and 415A in March of 1993 in the course of your duties with UNPROFOR in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you provide these documents to me prior to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are these two exhibits authentic copies of the documents you received at the time during the war?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The hand-written English translation, do you know how it was created, that is, what organisation or entity created it?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it was created by the interpreter cell in my battalion headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This document, Mr. President, for the record, it is a protest signed by Dusko Grubesic, and I would like to read portions and ask the witness to help us all identify some of the locations referred to in the document. If the map, which has a number, I'm sure, by now --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D416 on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could move it up slightly and zoom in so we have a closer picture, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The protest is dated 13 March, 1993. "Protest because of breaking the cease-fire. We are protesting to ECMM and UNPROFOR because Muslim armed forces, instead of all agreements, still breaking the cease-fire. On 12 March, 1993, at 2040 hours they were shooting from machine gun, M-48, on our positions in village Kula." Could you please indicate the area known as Kula? And are you indicating an area immediately to the east, north-east of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's Busovaca, there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Kula, if you could indicate it, once again? Thank you. Second bullet point: "From regions Pezici and Gornji Rovna, they provoced our units all night from personal weapons on our positions in villages Donja Rovna, Bare, and Roske Stijene. Muslim forces were shooting from anti-aircraft machine gun about 05 --"

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And here, Mr. President, it says 0503 hours in the translation, but I see in the original it is 0530 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "On this same locations." First, could you indicate the locations identified as sources of fire on the 12th of March, 1993, namely Pezici and Gornji Rovna?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Pezici and Gornji Rovna are here on very high ground, Pezici and Gornji Rovna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you indicate Donji Rovna and Bare on this exhibit, Exhibit D416?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Donji Rovna is here and Bare is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Third bullet point: "At 2230 hours they opened the fire from direction of Merdani on our locations in village Gavrne Kuce. They were using fire munitions and burned two Muslim houses in this location. Send this protest to ECMM, UN and BH army, commander of brigade, Dusko Grubesic." Could you indicate the village of Merdani?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Merdani is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. There is a reference in this document to use of an anti-aircraft machine gun for ground assault. What is an anti-aircraft machine gun; or is itself explanatory? Can you describe the type of gun?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: There are many different types, but in Bosnia they generally used a 12.7 millimetre, which is about half an inch, machine gun, which is designed for shooting down aircraft. It has a very high rate of fire, and obviously quite large calibre. And it has a very long barrel which allows it to project these the projectiles very high into the sky, they hit aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could assist, Mr. President, I have another document to distribute. It is a similar document, another protest, there is a BSC original and a hand-written English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D417, D417A for the hand-written English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you examine these documents, please? Do you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are they also documents that you received during your service in UNPROFOR in Bosnia during the war?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are they true copies or authentic copies of those documents which you provided to me prior to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the BSC original there's a hand-written notation in the upper right-hand corner; do you see where it reads "This fax for the attention captain M. J. Dundas-Whatley"?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This is a shorter document, Mr. President, and I will read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's again titled -- first of all, it is dated 14 March 1993, a protest against the breach of the cease-fire agreement. "We protest to the ECMM and the UN because the Bosnian army forces, despite everyday meetings concerning the realisation of what has been agreed, are breaking the truce. On 14 March, 1993 the BH army forces were engaged in provocative fire from small arms from the direction of Pezici and" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And Mr. President, from the original, I think it is reasonably clear, the second location is Vranjska, V-R-A-N-J-S-K-A, although it is very difficult to read, but I do believe it is Vranjska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Towards the positions at Roske Stijene and Kovacevac and Donji Rovna. From 1213 hours to 1300 hours they were firing from an anti-aircraft machine gun. We are informing about this the gentlemen from the ECMM, UN and the BH army." Signed brigade commander, Dusko Grubesic. I believe there is only one location Mr. Whatley mentioned in this document which hasn't already been identified for the Court -- well, actually there are two. First of all, there's indication that fire came from Pezici, which you; could you identify that one more time? Thank you. And Vranjska, where is Vranjska?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Vitez in relation to Vranjska? Can you move the map slightly down? There we go. So Vitez is where you're indicating now, and Vranjska is to the south-east. The fire was towards the positions, among others, of Donji Rovna, and Kovacevac. Do you see Kovacevac, between Pezici and Bare? It is not highlighted. Thank you. Did you keep up your diary after you had been in the country in Bosnia for a period of time, or was there no longer time to keep a narrative diary?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: I kept a diary from the day I arrived until the beginning of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After January, 1993, did you keep any abbreviated notes?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, when I came back from leave at the -- I was away for two weeks in January, and when I came back towards the end of January I didn't keep a diary, so all I maintained was my army notebooks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention to specific events now in April of 1993. And if you need to refer to your contemporaneous notes, with the Court's leave, you may do so; but please indicate when you are, so it is clear in the record. First I would like to direct your attention to the 7th of April, 1993. Did you meet with the BH army commander in Kruscica on that day?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Vance-Owen Peace Plan mentioned by him?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a reference in your notebook to this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, there are three things in my notebook which relate to the Vance -- relate to this. The first one, the commander, the Bosnian army commander in Kruscica is asking me to provide him with a written version of the Vance-Owen Plan, because he hadn't had it. He then went onto say "Never under command HVO," and then he said, "Muslim provinces full."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a lot of meetings on a daily basis with different people, different headquarters and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without your notebook, would you be able to tell us that those things were said in this meeting on the 7th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Without this notebook I can remember very little of the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From five years ago.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Five-and-a-half.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Five-and-a-half, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the next day, the 8th of April, 1993. Did you visit the town of Travnik on April 8th?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I attended, this was my third meeting that day, and I attended a joint meeting of the Bosnian army and the HVO in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn of a troop movement on the 8th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait one moment. What did you learn in this meeting on the 8th of April, 1993, concerning a troop movement?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Colonel Filipovic, the HVO commander in Travnik, told me "five hundred soldiers from Visoko to barracks in Travnik." He then went on to say "2100 hours," referring to the previous evening, "Flag burned," in brackets, "Croat". He then told me that the HVO command was now going to be in Dolac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the first thing you recounted from your notebook, that 500 troops had moved from Visoko to Travnik; were there any HVO troops in Visoko that you knew of, at the time?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: They --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or did you have an understanding as to whose troops these were that would have moved from Visoko to Travnik barracks?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: There may well have been HVO troops in Visoko, but this is not a reference to HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you determine that?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Because Filipovic told me about it, because he was concerned about it. And in addition, because they went to the barracks in Travnik, which was not a HVO barracks, it was a Bosnian army barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a movement of 500 Bosnian army soldiers to Travnik on the 8th of April, would that be considered a large troop movement in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it would. That would be quite a convoy of buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you learned at this meeting that the HVO had moved its headquarters out of the town of Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW DUNDAS-WHATLEY
utterances.text: That's correct. I think they moved that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask that another map be marked, unless --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President, what our hours will be for the balance of the day, but if we're going to proceed I would be moving on to another map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're going to stop at 5.30, because the interpreters began working at 9.30 this morning. We must stop at 5.30 if you want to begin another subject, otherwise we can stop right now. As you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We would probably consume a couple of minutes getting this map situated on the ELMO properly; so I suggest we break, and when we begin tomorrow we will have it in place and save the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. The Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.27 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 29th day of October, 1998. 20 21 22 23 24 25
